Persistent expertise

Across successive filing seasons, the experience left in household submissions can diminish as customers complete more work, while novices retain the option of purchasing instruction when future professional earnings justify its cost. In the shared-expertise extension with persistent human research, the budget and labor market imply w+qξ≥BR/Ew+q\xi\ge B_R/Ew+qξ≥BR​/E, so a small qualified population supports a strong training incentive through the research fund’s demand for scarce expertise.

Along a global feasible career path with nonnegative qualification values, that scarcity condition prevents expertise from remaining arbitrarily close to zero, because study below replacement would force the value equation downward too quickly to preserve a nonnegative career value. Proposition J.1 gives an explicit positive population bound even with M=0M=0M=0, and a bounded service-demand envelope then gives an upper wage bound.

For settled customer environments, eventual human research labor weakly rises exactly when service hours released at the old wage cover the lost expert supply evaluated at the old training incentive. Through that comparison, customer preparation determines the coefficient of subsequent frontier growth, while the productivity of the complete research method determines its exponent.

Evaluating both changes at the old wage gives a common price for comparing the work released and the expertise lost, before the new market adjusts. Their difference determines the direction of that adjustment, while eventual research labor translates it into the number of packets produced at each frontier, so customer preparation can change the speed along a growth path whose production exponent stays the same.

Complete methods

Weak links

Jones and Tonetti (2026) studies complementary tasks with substitution elasticity below one. Our generation-and-validation exponent follows separately from the sum of required inputs.

Within the CES task economy of Jones and Tonetti (2026), substitution elasticity below one leaves output constrained by remaining tasks when a fixed subset becomes arbitrarily productive. Their dynamic extension also automates idea production, linking innovation to further automation while weak links slow its consequences, and our serial research methods follow each required stage through a sum of generation and validation inputs.

Within that sum, the stage whose input requirement declines more slowly dominates the eventual requirement per completed packet. Factoring the smaller exponent from aHa_HaH​ or aMa_MaM​ leaves a positive bounded factor, giving the complete-method exponents above and a direct route from stage-level productivity to packet cost.

Within a method, completion requires both stages, so the smaller productivity exponent governs the input requirement that remains costly longest. Across complete methods, the fund can choose the cheaper route, so the larger eventual exponent can govern the selected cost under bounded input prices, giving the minimum within each method and the maximum across available methods distinct economic roles.

Levels and rates

For a fixed resource scale kkk, the exponent β\betaβ compares effective research productivity with idea difficulty. When 0<β<10<\beta<10<β<1, a larger frontier produces a larger absolute increment whose size still falls relative to the frontier already reached, so accelerating gains in levels coexist with declining proportional growth (fig. 11).

In human research, changes in the wage also enter proportional growth, with g˙A/gA=(ϵH−ϕ−1)gA−w˙/(w+qξ)\dot g_A/g_A=(\epsilon_H-\phi-1)g_A-\dot w/(w+q\xi)g˙​A​/gA​=(ϵH​−ϕ−1)gA​−w˙/(w+qξ). When wages fall, the budget purchases more research, while rising scarcity earnings absorb some productivity gains, connecting the career path to the growth rate beyond the scalar exponent comparison.

Holding the initial frontier and research resource scale fixed allows us to follow how the timing of new capability changes the research it supports. Immediate use, gradual absorption, and a minimum research duration pass the same improvement into subsequent work at different dates, which changes the connection between today’s discovery and tomorrow’s productive tools.

At the critical productivity exponent, either positive timing requirement lowers the eventual exponential rate below the rate supplied by immediate use, because each new improvement takes time to contribute fully to the next. Increasing the absorption time or minimum duration lengthens that passage, connecting the implicit growth-rate equations to a concrete delay in the production of subsequent advances.

Research duration

Under gradual absorption, effective research capability rrr approaches the current frontier with time scale ℓ>0\ell>0ℓ>0, giving recent improvements a continuously increasing role in production. Below η=1+ϕ\eta=1+\phiη=1+ϕ, the power asymptotic survives, while at equality the limiting exponential rate solves g(1+ℓg)η=kg(1+\ell g)^\eta=kg(1+ℓg)η=k, and higher elasticities retain a finite production endpoint.

Under a positive minimum duration τ\tauτ, today’s research can use only capability available at least one cycle earlier, so each interval inherits bounded inputs from the completed interval before it. Applying the method of steps then gives a finite frontier at every finite date, while supercritical productivity still yields growth whose double logarithm rises asymptotically at rate τ−1log⁡[η/(1+ϕ)]\tau^{-1}\log[\eta/(1+\phi)]τ−1log[η/(1+ϕ)].

During each such interval, research uses a capability history already produced, and the improvements it creates enter a later cycle, letting us bound production one completed interval at a time. Gradual absorption instead begins incorporating a recent improvement continuously, so its lag preserves a different connection between current frontier gains and the capability contributing to current research.

At the threshold, the fixed-duration exponential rate solves ge(1+ϕ)gτ=kge^{(1+\phi)g\tau}=kge(1+ϕ)gτ=k, which differs from the gradual-absorption equation because the two timing technologies pass improvements into production differently. Pages 53–56 give the classifications and proofs behind this comparison.

Resources and continuation

Research resources

Aghion, Jones, and Jones (2019) distinguishes automation in goods production from automation in ideas, connecting research inputs to the economy’s growth possibilities.

Distinguishing automation of goods from automation of ideas, as Aghion, Jones, and Jones (2019) does, directs attention to the resources that research uses while improving future production. In our autonomous research law, integration gives an exact resource clock, with cumulative effort required to reach a frontier on the left and available research purchasing power on the right. If budgets and compute prices scale with frontier exponents βB\beta_BβB​ and βq\beta_qβq​, the finite-arrival threshold becomes pM+βB−βq>1+ϕp_M+\beta_B-\beta_q>1+\phipM​+βB​−βq​>1+ϕ.

Human research also faces the physical bound LR≤EL_R\le ELR​≤E, so additional expenditure can bid up wages when existing expertise is already employed, with subsequent entry determined by private training. For a technology whose frontier coordinate has a finite endpoint, completion of the public program leaves a residual implementation occupation, whose earnings provide the continuation qualification value used in the preceding career problem.

With that continuation, research completion becomes an absorbing activity state while wages, study, and lifetime values continue in calendar time, linking the value of expertise before completion to the work remaining after the research program has ended.
